q: [71st BPSC-style] Which of the following subjects is in the Concurrent List?
explanation: Education moved State→Concurrent by the 42nd Amendment (1976) (with forests, weights & measures, wildlife protection, administration of justice). Police/public order = State; foreign affairs = Union.

q: India is described as 'quasi-federal' primarily because:
options: The Constitution tilts toward a strong Centre in emergencies, appointments and amendment processes while retaining dual polity
explanation: Wheare's 'quasi-federal': dual polity + single Constitution/citizenship, indestructible union of destructible states, Emergency's unitary conversion, Governor as Centre's agent, Union-dominated amendment. Not a confederation — states can't secede.

q: The Governor of a state is appointed by:
options: The President on the advice of the state CM
explanation: Art 155: the President appoints Governors (in practice the Union Cabinet's choice); tenure 5 years at the President's pleasure (Art 156) — the federal flashpoint Sarkaria/Punchhi sought to soften.

q: In the case where the SC struck down the dissolution of the Bihar Legislative Assembly (2005) on the Governor's mala fide recommendation, the case is:
options: State of Bihar v. Union of India
Rameshwar Prasad v. Union of India
S.R. Bommai v. Union of India
explanation: Rameshwar Prasad (2006): the Governor's report recommending Bihar's Assembly dissolution was mala fide — dissolution unconstitutional; floor-test principle reiterated (Bommai's child). Bihar's gift to federal jurisprudence.

q: Allocation of seats in the Rajya Sabha to states is provided in the:
explanation: 4th Schedule = RS seat allocation (Bihar 16) — 71st BPSC Q62 tested this matching. 2nd = salaries/emoluments; 3rd = forms of oath; 5th = scheduled areas.

q: The Finance Commission is constituted under:
explanation: Art 280: FC every 5 years (or earlier); 15th FC (N.K. Singh) awarded 41% devolution (2021-26); 16th FC (Arvind Panagariya) from 2025 for 2026-31. Art 281 merely says the President lays FC recommendations before Parliament.

q: In the GST Council, the voting weightage of the Centre and states is:
options: Equal voice for all members without voting
Centre 1/3, states 2/3; decisions by 3/4 of weighted votes
explanation: Art 279A: Union 1/3 of total votes, states collectively 2/3; decisions need 3/4 weighted votes — the states hold aggregate veto power. SC (Mohit Minerals, 2022): recommendations aren't binding legislation per se.

q: Residuary powers in India are vested in:
explanation: Art 248 + Union List Entry 97: the Union holds residuary powers (unlike USA/Australia where states do). Cyber law's early days exemplified Union reach via Entry 97.

q: The Inter-State Council was established in 1990 on the recommendation of:
explanation: Sarkaria Commission (1988 report) → ISC via Art 263 (Presidential Order 1990). Punchhi (2010) refined Centre-state relations; Rajamannar (1969, Tamil Nadu) wanted ISC-like bodies earlier.

q: Under Art 3, a bill reorganising a state requires:
options: Only the President's recommendation and Parliament's simple-majority law; the state's views are not binding
explanation: Art 3: Parliament's law (simple majority) on the President's recommendation; the affected state legislature's views are not binding — 'indestructible union of destructible states' (contrast the USA's indestructible states).

q: The 9th Schedule was added by the 1st Amendment (1951) largely to protect:
options: Land-reform legislation — including Bihar's zamindari-abolition acts
explanation: Bihar Land Reforms litigation triggered the 1st Amendment's 9th Schedule (land-reform immunity). I.R. Coelho (2007): post-1973 9th-Schedule laws are judicially reviewable against basic structure.

q: Which pair is correctly matched? (Allocation of seats in the councils of states; forms of oath; anti-defection; languages)
options: RS seats — 4th Schedule; oath — 3rd; anti-defection — 10th; languages — 8th
explanation: 71st Q62 tested exactly this: RS allocation = 4th, oath = 3rd, anti-defection = 10th, languages = 8th. (2nd = salaries; 5th/6th = scheduled areas/tribes.)

q: Inter-state river water disputes are resolved by tribunals under:
options: Article 262 — Parliament's law (Inter-State Water Disputes Act 1956); tribunal awards exclude SC jurisdiction
explanation: Art 262: Parliament may exclude SC/other jurisdiction over inter-state water disputes — the 1956 Act's tribunals (Cauvery, Krishna, Mahadayi); the 2019 amendment creates a single permanent tribunal. Bihar angle: Kosi/Gandak pacts with Nepal are international, not inter-state.

q: The Sarkaria Commission's key recommendation on Governors was:
options: Appointment of an eminent person (not active politician), removal only by impeachment-like process, and non-arbitrariness
explanation: Sarkaria (1988): eminent non-partisan persons, active politicians avoided, fixed tenure conventions, removal via due process. Punchhi added security of tenure recommendations. Neither implemented in practice.

q: 'Cooperative federalism' as a judicial idiom was most famously invoked in:
options: S.R. Bommai v. Union of India
State of West Bengal v. Union of India
explanation: Bommai (1994): federalism = basic structure; Art 356 judicially reviewable; floor tests mandatory; 'cooperative federalism' as the governing spirit — the case that tamed President's rule.

q: Which Schedule distributes powers over 'Forests'?
options: State List only till 1976; now Concurrent
explanation: Forests: State List → Concurrent (42nd Amdt 1976) (with education, weights & measures, wildlife, justice administration, population control).

q: The 15th Finance Commission's vertical devolution to states was:
explanation: 15th FC (N.K. Singh): 41% vertical devolution (from 42% after J&K's reorganisation). Horizontal criteria: income distance 45%, population 15%, area 15%, demographic performance 12.5%, forest ecology 10% — Bihar ranks first on income distance, making it a top gainer.

q: Zonal Councils were created by:
explanation: Zonal Councils = statutory (States Reorganisation Act 1956): 5 zones; chaired by the Union Home Minister; Bihar sits in the Eastern Zone (with WB, Odisha, Jharkhand + Sikkim's 2017 addition). ISC (Art 263) is constitutional — the classic distinction.

q: Under Article 200, when a state bill is presented to the Governor, he may:
options: Return it to the state legislature repeatedly
Assent, withhold, or reserve for the President
explanation: Art 200: the Governor may assent, withhold, or reserve for the President (and may return a non-Money bill once for reconsideration). Under Art 201, the President may assent, withhold, or direct return. The 2024-25 SC timelines on 'deemed assent' for pending bills stem from here.

q: Kerala's suit against the Centre over state borrowing limits (2023) was filed under:
explanation: Kerala's fiscal-autonomy suit (borrowing-limit restrictions; net-borrowing ceiling) invoked Art 131 — the modern Centre-state litigation frontier; SC entertained the dispute — cooperative federalism's stress-test in 2024-25 news.

q: The phrase 'Union of States' in Article 1 conveys:
options: An indestructible union of destructible states — the federation is not the result of an agreement; states cannot secede
explanation: Ambedkar: 'Union' chosen over 'Federation' — no agreement, no secession; Art 3 makes states destructible while the Union endures. BPSC's most repeated polity-one-liner.

q: Which state's Legislative Assembly dissolution case is the landmark on Governors' mala fide reports?
explanation: Bihar 2005 (Rameshwar Prasad): Governor Buta Singh's report mala fide → dissolution unconstitutional. Karnataka 1989 fed Bommai; UP/MP cases are later applications.

q: The 42nd Amendment (1976) transferred which subjects from the State to the Concurrent List?
explanation: 42nd Amdt: education, forests, weights & measures, protection of wild animals/birds, administration of justice, population control & family planning → Concurrent. Five subjects also moved to Union List.

q: Bihar's share in the central divisible pool under the 15th Finance Commission is approximately:
explanation: Bihar receives ~10% (10.06%) of the devolution — the largest per the horizontal formula (highest income distance). UP ~18% leads in absolute terms; Bihar's ~10% is second-tier — the 'fiscal federalism favours Bihar' line.

q: The Punchhi Commission (2010) on Centre-state relations recommended:
options: Fixed tenure for Governors; Art 356 only after a floor test — a deep federal toolkit
explanation: Punchhi (2010): Governor's fixed tenure; Art 356 as a last resort after floor test; inter-state commerce reforms; ISC activation — the Sarkaria-plus package.
